THE PROMISE
What if we gave 10,000 people back just one hour a week?
One hour lost to unnecessary approvals, missing information or rules that make good work harder.
Over 46 working weeks, that is 460,000 hours.
What could our people do with that time?
Serve customers better?
Solve problems?
Learn?
Build something we haven’t even thought of?
Let’s unlock human potential by removing the organizational barriers we create and keep in place.
When my friend Matt Chalmers reposted my previous article, he wrote:
“I see much more than a role or a title here ... especially not a "Chief Officer". I see a mindset, growing in organisations newly biased towards "People & Transformation".”
That stayed with me.
A mindset becomes meaningful through the decisions we make, the barriers we remove and the responsibility we accept.
Here is how I would turn that mindset into measurable commitments.
LESS FRICTION
Objective: Remove the barriers that waste human time.
→ Key Result: Within twelve months, remove 30% of the time lost to our ten biggest organizational barriers.
→ KPI: Friction hours per employee.
PEOPLE EMPOWERMENT & MORE AGENCY
Objective: Give people the information, tools and authority to act.
→ Key Results: Move half of the decisions we unnecessarily escalate to the people competent to make them. Cut median decision waiting time by 40%.
→ KPIs: Decision-at-source rate. Median decision waiting time.
A VOICE THAT COUNTS
Objective: Make speaking up lead to visible action.
→ Key Results: Reduce median waiting time for a first personal response by 50%. Test or implement at least 25% of viable suggestions — with everyone able to see what happened and why.
→ KPIs: Median time to first personal response. Voice-to-action rate.
POTENTIAL PUT TO WORK
Objective: Discover and use the capabilities our job titles conceal.
→ Key Result: Fill 20% of suitable project opportunities with internal talent we hadn’t previously recognized.
→ KPI: Share of suitable project opportunities filled through newly discovered internal talent.
These are proposed targets for the first twelve months. We would establish the baseline, agree the commitments, and verify the results with the people doing the work.
The KPIs tell us where we stand.
The OKRs commit us to changing it.
And the test is simple:
Are people more able to do great work today than they were a year ago?
That is the promise I want to be held accountable for.
libfile_3ab6bd800f0c81918737556f2e3fa887:
Oh, we’re sooo good at working around our organizations.

We should all have #Workarounder next to our job title.

Chasing approvals.
Calling someone who knows someone.
Finding another way because the magnificent new tool doesn’t quite do the job.

And somehow, we get it done.

Our ingenuity keeps the work going.
It can also hide where the organization needs to change.

Most rules started with a good intention.
Safety. Quality. Consistency. Accountability.

Those things matter.

But ten individually sensible rules don’t necessarily make one sensible system.

When we discover a workaround, we have a choice.

We can close it and wait for the next one.

Or we can sit down with the people doing the work and ask:
What are you trying to achieve?
What makes the approved route difficult?
What risk does the rule protect us from?
How can we make good work possible while keeping that protection?

Sometimes the answer is a clearer process.
Sometimes it’s a missing tool.
Sometimes we need to change who can decide — or reconsider the rule itself.

We need to understand which.

A workaround is a clue: there may be a gap between how we designed the work and what the work actually
requires.

Let’s get curious before we get corrective.

I have to remind myself of that almost every day.
My first impulse often knows the way to drama.
Curiosity helps me find out what’s actually going on.

We say we want empowerment.
So what are we actively doing to prevent it?

Then comes the work of leadership:

Bring the right people together.
Agree what needs to change.
Take responsibility for changing it.
Check whether it actually helps.

Did we remove the need for the workaround?
Did we preserve the safety and quality we need?
Are people more able to do great work?

A better workaround is still a workaround.
My ambition is to make it unnecessary.

Imagine what people could do with more of that ingenuity available for customers, problems worth solving
and ideas worth trying.

Perhaps that’s our Monday question:

What can we change today so that our teams go home saying:

“Today went really well.
Things keep getting better.”


These reflections draw on my experience across industries, roles and organizations — including my own choices as a leader.

LINKEDIN-TEASER
Let’s fix our friction-filled peopleware.
Don’t optimize the humans.
Remove the friction.
Then let’s see what they can do.
YOUR MOST WASTED RESOURCE IS HUMAN.
And I’m looking for the company that’s serious about changing that.
YOUR MOST WASTED RESOURCE IS HUMAN.
And I'm looking for the company that's serious about changing that.
I have been talking about people for a very long time.
Two of the strongest slides I ever put on a stage said:
“It’s all about people, and what those people do.”
“Digital business is a people business.”
I meant every word.
People were never an afterthought in my work. They were the point.
But I didn't know then what I know now.
Because there is a difference between believing in people — and standing beside them at six 
in the morning.
I left the ivory tower.
For years, I worked in digital transformation.
APIs. Platforms. Ecosystems. Organizational change.
I wrote books about it. I taught it. I stood on stages and talked about it.
Then I left.
I put on work clothes and became a facility technician.
And somewhere between early shifts, broken machines, dirty hands and conversations over 
coffee, my understanding of organizations changed.
Not my belief that people matter.
My understanding of how much of them organizations never get to see.
I will always be grateful that I was given the opportunity to enter this world. It taught me 
more about organizations than I ever expected to learn.
The people our ease of life rests on.
I met people I had barely met in my previous professional life.
Not because they weren't there.
Because I wasn't where they were.
People who clean our buildings. Repair our machines. Prepare our food. Keep our 
infrastructure running.
People on whose shoulders much of our comfortable ease of life rests.
And I developed a profound respect for them.
For people mastering their lives on salaries many executives would barely notice.
For people largely cut off from the kind of education I had learned to take for granted.
For people living with existential financial worries — and rarely complaining about them.
I have met people for whom signing documents they cannot fully understand has become a 
normal part of life.
People who cannot negotiate on equal terms because they do not have the language.
People who are not asking whether their next job will fulfil them.
They are simply glad to have a job.
They show up. Every day.
And they receive nowhere near the recognition they deserve.
“Wie geht’s?”
Here in Switzerland, we have a little ritual.
We meet someone and ask: “Wie geht’s?”
How are you?
And the answer is almost always: “Gut.”
Good.
Because most of the time, nobody really wants to know.
I do.
I want to know what comes after “Gut.”
What makes your work unnecessarily difficult.
What you're worried about.
What you have learned not to say because experience taught you that nobody would listen.
What you know about this organization that nobody in the boardroom knows.
What you could do if somebody actually gave you the opportunity.
And whenever I can, I try to help.
What if we actually meant “People First”?
I have become convinced that most organizations are sitting on an extraordinary amount of 
human intelligence they never use.
Intelligence doesn't begin with a university degree.
Creativity doesn't belong to management.
Leadership isn't determined by an org chart.
And the person cleaning a machine may understand what is wrong with the process better 
than the person who designed it.
So imagine what would happen if a large organization started taking that seriously.
Really seriously.
Not another employee survey.
Not another values poster.
Not another People First slide.
But a fundamental assumption:
The people working here have the intelligence, capability and heart to
take this organization to places management alone never could.
Then let's build around that assumption.
Let's find the friction — and remove it.
Let's give people agency.
Let's listen to the people closest to the work.
Let's make language a bridge instead of a barrier.
Let's stop treating the workforce as a cost to optimize and start treating it as the enormous 
reservoir of human capability it actually is.
And now there is AI.
It is time.
AI will become better at things we once believed were uniquely ours.
Faster. More knowledgeable. More analytical. More productive.
We shouldn't fight that.
We should meet it with the one thing AI can never become: human.
With empathy. With courage. With dignity. With intuition. With responsibility. With the 
ability to truly care about another human being.
For decades, organizations have tried to make people more like machines: predictable, 
measurable, standardized, efficient.
Maybe it's time we did the opposite.
Let machines become better machines.
Let humans become better humans.
That's the transformation I'm interested in.
So here is what I know now.
There is one role that could make me leave the boiler room again.
A role with the mandate to take everything I have learned here and combine it with 
everything I learned in the decades before.
Call it Chief People & Transformation Officer.
The title doesn't matter much to me.
The mandate does.
The mandate to go from the boiler room to the boardroom — and back again.
To find the intelligence an organization isn't using.
To find the friction that prevents people from doing their best work.
And to remove it.
To find out what this organization could become if we started taking its people seriously.
Really seriously.
Only call me if you mean it.
Don't call me because you need someone to run HR.
Don't call me because People & Culture needs a refresh.
And don't call me because the employee engagement score needs to go up three points.
Call me if you're prepared to mean it.
Because then we are going to ask uncomfortable questions.
We are going to listen to people we haven't listened to before.
We are going to challenge things that have been “just the way we do things” for twenty years.
We are going to move decision-making closer to where the work actually happens.
We are going to remove friction.
And yes: things will change.
A lot.
And if nobody calls?
That's perfectly fine.
I have a job. I have made a commitment. And I intend to honour it.
Tomorrow morning, I'll put on my work clothes and go read the heating meters.
I'll fix something that's broken.
I'll have coffee with people I've grown to deeply respect.
And I'll probably ask someone: “Wie geht’s?”
And when they say “Gut” —
I'll still want to know what comes after that.

TEASER
One week in a gardening team.
Already dispensing expert advice.
I’d cleaned ships’ cargo holds with a fire hose.
How hard could a leaf blower be?
The leaves had a different opinion.
Fortunately, my colleagues had patience.
And the spade stayed on the ground.
I mistook their mastery for the simplicity of the task.
How often do we do that when we lead?
THE DUNNING–KRUGER APPROXIMATION.
A little knowledge. A lot of confidence. And some very uncooperative leaves.



THE DUNNING–KRUGER APPROXIMATION
Oh, how many times have I done this?
One week in a gardening team.
Already full of very clever advice.
Very clever.
Very early.
Luckily, the colleague in this picture seems kindly disposed towards me.
She’s listening.
The spade is still resting on the ground.
I count that as a good start.
The leaves disagreed
Have you ever tried moving a large pile of leaves in one specific direction with a high-powered leaf blower on a busy street?
I used to clean ships’ cargo holds with a fire hose.
Surely I had some transferable skills.
The leaves disagreed.
There I was, feeling like a complete idiot, hoping my colleagues would give me time to learn.
Then there’s the grass trimmer.
In experienced hands, it looks effortless. Learning that control takes months. Until then, enthusiasm can leave quite a mark on the property.
I had watched people do these things and thought I understood the work.
I mistook their mastery for the simplicity of the task.
“Now I’ve got it.”
I’ve spent a considerable part of my life learning things.
Guitar. Unicycling. Juggling. Steel mace. Kettlebells. Motorcycling. Programming. Speaking on stage. Teaching. New jobs.
Again and again, I’ve had that wonderful moment:
“Now I’ve got it.”
Usually shortly before discovering what I hadn’t got yet.
A different situation. A bad day. Something that worked yesterday suddenly refusing to cooperate.
Being good at one thing has never given me a free pass into the next. I still have to learn the work.
What I do bring with me is a growing willingness to question the feeling that I already understand.
That feeling can be remarkably convincing.
A little knowledge. A very complete explanation.
Dunning and Kruger studied how people assess their own abilities. Their original research found substantial overestimation among participants with low performance in the tested domains, linked in part to difficulty recognising their own errors.
My gardening adventures aren’t a psychological diagnosis. But they give me a very personal reason to examine the gap between confidence and understanding.
The familiar “Mount Stupid” and “Valley of Despair” illustration captures something I recognise in my learning: early certainty, the discovery of complexity, and a slower, more grounded understanding.
It’s an illustration, not the curve measured in the original study. And the vertical axis is confidence. Our knowledge doesn’t necessarily disappear when our confidence does.
Sometimes we’re finally learning enough to see what we’ve been missing.

Murphy arranges the site visit
People doing the work often have every reason to say:
“You don’t understand what this job actually takes.”
Knowing the job title isn’t knowing the work.
Even having done the job isn’t the same as doing it here, with this team, these tools, and these conditions.
And when we finally visit to see for ourselves?
Murphy arranges the visit.
Everything runs beautifully.
Or everyone is having a break.
“Looks straightforward.”
Excellent. We’ve now mistaken a quiet moment for a complete understanding.
The work it takes to make things look easy is often the work we never see.
The bottle-cleaner trap
One person cleans 100 bottles an hour.
Ten people clean 1,000.
Beautiful arithmetic.
Do we have ten cleaning stations?
Enough water pressure?
Who supplies the bottles?
Who checks them?
Where do they go afterwards?
The calculation could be right. We need to establish whether its assumptions hold.
We multiplied the people.
We haven’t checked whether the work can scale.
And that brings me to a question that matters enormously in leadership:
Who estimates the effort — especially when I’m already convinced I understand the job?
My confidence isn’t an estimate.
Let’s build one with the people who will actually do the work.
Otherwise, we risk a familiar sequence:
“I knew how long it should take.
I didn’t ask the people doing it.
And when it took longer, I questioned their performance.”
Perhaps I should have questioned my estimate first.
My unchecked assumption can become somebody else’s supposed performance problem.
How do we practise Humility — and avoid the “I know it all” trap?
For me, it starts with treating “That looks easy” as a reason to ask a question.
“What do you understand about this work that I haven’t learned to see yet?”
Then I need to stay long enough to hear the answer.
Observe more than one convenient moment. Ask about the difficult days, the exceptions, the preparation, and the recovery afterwards.
Build estimates with the people doing the work. Make the assumptions visible. Find out what depends on somebody else.
And when reality differs from the plan, investigate together.
What did we miss?
What changed?
What needs to happen now?
Let’s get curious before we get corrective.
I have to remind myself of that almost every day.
My first impulse often knows the way to drama.
Curiosity helps me find out what’s actually going on.
Our internal software loves a simple explanation.
A little familiarity.
A plausible story.
“Got it.”
Dunning and Kruger give us a reason to pause before trusting that feeling.
My internal human software has declared the problem understood.
Reality hasn’t signed off yet.
So how do I outsmart my own shortcut?
#Humility.
“What am I missing?”
“Who sees something I don’t?”
“Can you show me?”
And then comes the difficult bit:
Letting the answers change my mind.

I LOOOVE UNDERCOVER BOSS.

There. I said it.

Give me a CEO with a ridiculous beard, an unfamiliar name badge and absolutely no idea how to operate the fryer.

I’m in.

Call her Kathleen. Call him Earl.

And when Kathleen gets $20,000 so her daughter can go to college?

Or Earl gets the car he desperately needs — and someone finally sees that having a job hasn’t stopped him from having nowhere to sleep?

Yep. Tears.

Mine too.

I’ve never been the CEO of a giant corporation. But I recognise that urge:

Let me do something.
We can make this better.
Surely we can bloody make this better.

What gets me even more is the moment before the cheque.

When the boss struggles with something their colleague makes look ridiculously easy.

When they discover how much knowledge lives behind that counter.

When someone tells them what it takes to get through a shift. And then through the rest of the day.

You can almost see an entire explanation of the world falling apart.

“Oh God.
I had no idea.”

#HUMILITY.

I know a little about that bit.

After years of digital programmes, coaching and conference stages, I picked up a grass trimmer.

My colleagues could do things I couldn’t.
See things I didn’t.
Anticipate problems I hadn’t even noticed.

I brought plenty of experience.

I still needed someone to show me how to do the job.

Again.
And sometimes again.

#THANKYOUFORYOURPATIENCE.

That’s why I love watching the boss become a beginner.

For a moment, they need the very people who usually need their permission.

And something opens.

Now comes the question that keeps me busy:

What happens when the beard comes off?

Back at the desk.
Back in the meetings.
Back where decisions are made.

Does what we’ve seen change what we do?

The gift matters. To that person, it may matter enormously.

And there are other people behind other counters.

Could we make it easier for them to tell us what we haven’t understood?

Could we give them the tools, time and authority their work actually requires?

Could we let their knowledge change our decisions?

I want to keep the tears.

And carry that AHA into Tuesday.

Because “I had no idea” can be a beautiful beginning.

“What am I going to do now that I know?”

That’s where leadership gets interesting.
